title: 📚 Second Age Annals — Historical Framework & Complete Culture Index (1–1437)
rawNotionMarkup: Creator-authorized comprehensive expansion • 21 November 2026. These annals develop Eryndor's entire 1,437-year Second Age with continent-specific and people-specific histories. The tone is dark, gritty and hopeful: suffering is real, institutions can fail, exploitation and warfare have lasting consequences, and hope comes from people working, protecting one another and changing unjust customs. Additions are revisable canon, not immutable revelations. This page is the chronological and continuity index for the associated continent annals and people-by-people ledger. ## Chronology and naming rules Global Ages mark planetwide historical intervals and disasters. Era names are continental and cultural, not universal. Only Avarra's historical three-era convention is currently fixed: Awakening, Second Age Years 1–321; Wonder, Years 322–1,321; Fire, Years 1,322–1,437. Elsewhere, these are only cross-referenced Avarran date labels. Tharvorn, Sahrad, Orundel and Vaelora may count and name their own eras differently; their local names and boundaries have not been fixed in this expansion. Avarran retroactive year numbers are used solely for comparison, not as proof that everyone used a common calendar. The First Age is of unknown length, had no eras and left no genuine surviving records. The moon-shattering Great Cataclysm ended it and began the Second Age. Some old lunar magical powers were permanently lost when source moons were destroyed; shattered fragments birthed new moons with new sources of lunar power; surviving magic could fluctuate dangerously. The world's independent Natural Magic / World's Breath is not lunar power. The old Ironspine ring existed long before the First Age. End of Second Age (Year 1,437): World-shaking earthquakes, globally amplified tenfold by the ancient Ironspine's vast deep roots, violently raised portions of Avarra's far-western lowlands and marshes into new mountains. Regional societies and settlements suffered immense casualties, yet no species became extinct; an unspecified magical force contributed to survival without cancelling the devastation. Do not define the earthquake's cause, the survival force or its connection to the First Throne. The exiled dark mages had created the southeastern Avarran Southern Wastes and volcano at the beginning of Year 1,322, and at the end of the era they restrained some of the intensified volcano's devastating power, unknowingly becoming more powerful. They had no external diplomacy, trade or alliances and survived well into the Third Age. The mages created the Orcs/Urakai sometime in the Third Age only, aiming first at Khazari strongholds and later Eldar and human kingdoms; exact means, date and military outcomes remain open. Goblins and Ogres may occur in the Second Age, but no Orcs do. ## What living through the Second Age actually meant The Second Age was not one era of universal darkness followed by universal sunlight. A sick child and an ingenious engineer could inhabit the same city; a court could fund healing while permitting debt bondage; a thriving magical trade road could be bordered by villages where magic was too expensive to use. Prosperity, corruption, war, famine, work, family and joy developed side by side. No people's temperament, religion, family size, birth rate, morality or occupation follows automatically from their species. No present-day city, dynasty, Seven Throne state or Fifth Age institution is automatically backdated by these annals. ## A historical sequence — Avarran Second Age-relative years ### Years 1–36: the broken guarantees When moon-based wards, weather predictions, protections and healings became unreliable, those with land, stores and guarded roads often did better than the vulnerable. Some lords charged for access to functioning enchanted wells; others opened grainhouses. Across Eryndor, practical navigators, midwives, stoneworkers, seed-keepers, rescue leaders and water-watchers became indispensable. The period's great fear was not that magic had vanished everywhere, but that it could no longer always be trusted. The Two-Hand Rule among some Khazari, Living Calendar methods among some Eldar and the Second Measure among some human communities gained force amid real losses. ### Years 37–104: salt, seed and shelter Across separate continents, people restored overland markers, ordinary canals, shore soundings and physically tested dwellings. A few rising governors tried to make rescue and food an inherited privilege, sparking labor refusals, underground distribution and violent repression. Other communities developed pooled emergency stores with public witnesses. The same population could contain wealthy profiteers and courageous neighbors; no universal humanitarian awakening occurred. ### Years 105–203: the politics of repair Better documentation of altered lunar magic let some communities experiment cautiously. In others, fearful magistrates prosecuted ordinary magic workers for catastrophes they had not caused. Mixed-species towns learned practical ways of regulating shared wells, fair weights and rescue duties even where their councils excluded entire neighborhoods. Coastal exchanges resumed unevenly, while some closed mountain, woodland and island communities remained suspicious of outsiders. ### Years 204–321: the last uncertainties of the Awakening Some regions achieved stable schools, markets and craft colleges; others continued to endure failing crops, dangerous routes or exploitative rulers. Avarran historians later grouped these generations into a 321-year Awakening. Outside Avarra, no one is required to have recognized that transition. The actual Year 321 / 322 date is the Avarran dividing line, not a world-spanning sudden event. ### Years 322–490: inventions with owners New lunar disciplines were understood and worked into irrigation, preservation, illumination, architecture, healing and communications. The first large-scale disputes of this period were often about access: royal monopolies, guild secrecy, toll rights and expensive education. Apprentices, translators and itinerant craftspeople sometimes spread knowledge despite bans. New inventions did not restore powers whose source moons had ceased to exist. ### Years 491–705: flourishing and fracture New towns and courts supported arts, scholarship, large family enterprises, healing and trade. Prosperity created debts as well as wealth. Some ambitious rulers expanded tax networks into independent villages; some subjects fled, negotiated rights or rebelled. River toll wars and local dynastic conflicts occurred in different continents but were not one coordinated east–west world war. In every case, ordinary food supply and human labor still mattered even to enchantment-rich cities. ### Years 706–930: the age of contested learning Temples, craft houses, observatories and independent schools disagreed over whether lunar power could be patented, inherited, licensed or held as sacred common knowledge. Some innovators were generous, some cruel; some critics were protectors and others opportunistic persecutors. Local histories include debt relief leagues, threatened archives, sanctuary houses, ruined workshops and new methods of teaching which did not require a patron noble. ### Years 931–1,119: the height and burden of Wonder Avarran accounts celebrate extraordinary building and scholarship, while tax records and travelers' memoirs describe exhausted laborers, guarded forest gates, predatory river tolls and communities displaced by celebrated projects. Some courts reformed themselves; others fell to succession struggles, creditor revolts or regional campaigning. No single monarch ruled the five continents. Each region's own annals explain its conflicts and the people who resisted them. ### Years 1,120–1,321: hard-won institutions For some communities, a century of prosperity gave birth to enduring craft traditions, public hospitals, navigational schools, seed exchanges, mixed-neighborhood councils or reliable engineering practices. For others, increasingly elaborate enchantments made government more secretive and access more unequal. Families, itinerants, soldiers, artisans and scholars imagined very different futures. The Era of Wonder's end did not mean a synchronized collapse across the globe. ### Years 1,322–1,436: the later Avarran Era of Fire At its opening, the exiled mages turned formerly fertile southeastern Avarran farmland into the Southern Wastes and created the volcano. Refugee histories, regional responses and later political shifts form part of the existing Era of Fire — Kingdoms, Peoples & Cultural Chronicle (Second Age, 1322–1437). Elsewhere, kingdoms continued farming, arguing, building, worshipping and fighting their own disputes. No other continent must have called this period “Fire.” ### Year 1,437: the breaking of an Age The worldwide earthquake catastrophe ended the Second Age, not simply an Avarran political dynasty or local era. Many communities had rebuilt painstakingly for centuries and now lost homes and records again. Their suffering was not a moral judgment or a magical punishment. The survival of peoples owes something to an as-yet-undefined magical force; neither its source nor operation is assigned by this history. The Third Age begins afterward, without any Orc settlements preceding it. ## Historical method and what these annals do not decide - Regional histories: Each continent's annal contains particular rulers, towns, legal struggles, wars, family and professional traditions, and people from many species. They are ancient polities and communities, not automatic predecessors of Fifth Age states. - People-by-people ledger: Named incidents connect these political histories to the lived experience of all 28 modeled peoples, with Drakari and Aelwyn included separately and Living Mountains remaining deliberately undated. - Worldbuilding choices still open: Precise borders, ancient population totals, dates of the First Throne and its Silence Below, the extinction-preventing force, all magical details not explicitly established, First Age accounts, later Orc origins' precise method, and Gloin's genealogy. - Campaign safeguard: This is out-of-character reference lore. It does not confer knowledge on Gloin Hammerfeld or change his paused scene at Hadrik Ironvein's desk in Karak-Varn, Autumn Day 22, Year 3,847 of the Era of Crowns, approximately 11:25 AM.
